109	**3.4 Complaint-Driven Investigations and Inquiry Letters (Ongoing)**
110	
111	In addition to proactive enforcement sweeps, the CPPA conducts investigations based on individual consumer complaints. The CPPA\'s complaint intake process allows California consumers to file complaints via an online portal on the CPPA\'s website (cppa.ca.gov) or by contacting the agency directly. The portal collects information regarding the nature of the alleged violation, the business involved, and supporting documentation such as correspondence with the business, screenshots, or copies of privacy requests and responses.
112	
113	When the CPPA determines that a complaint warrants further review, the Enforcement Division issues an \"Inquiry Letter\" to the business. An Inquiry Letter is not a finding of violation and does not constitute a formal accusation. Rather, it represents the first step in a potential enforcement action, serving as a mechanism for the CPPA to gather information and assess whether further investigation is warranted.
114	
115	The typical Inquiry Letter provides the business 30 business days to respond and requests the following categories of information:
116	
117	> \(a\) copies of the consumer\'s original request(s) and the business\'s response(s), including all correspondence and timestamps;
118	>
119	> \(b\) the business\'s written policies and procedures for handling consumer rights requests of the type at issue (e.g., deletion, access, correction, opt-out);
120	>
121	> \(c\) a list of all service providers and contractors to whom the consumer\'s personal information was disclosed in the prior 12 months; and
122	>
123	> \(d\) evidence that the business directed downstream recipients to delete or otherwise cease processing the consumer\'s data, as applicable.
124	
125	Failure to respond to an Inquiry Letter, or providing an incomplete or inadequate response, may result in the CPPA escalating the matter to a formal investigation. A formal investigation can lead to administrative proceedings and the imposition of fines up to \$2,500 per violation, or \$7,500 per intentional violation, along with compliance orders and injunctive relief.
126	
127	The CPPA has indicated publicly that it treats the responsiveness and good faith of businesses during the Inquiry Letter phase as a mitigating factor when determining penalties in any subsequent enforcement action. Conversely, the CPPA has stated that non-responsiveness, evasiveness, or the discovery of broader compliance issues during the inquiry process can serve as aggravating factors that increase both the scope of investigation and the severity of penalties.
128	
129	**CHG relevance.** CHG received an Inquiry Letter dated February 3, 2025 (Case No. CPPA-ENF-2025-01847), triggered by two consumer complaints filed on December 10, 2024, and December 28, 2024, respectively. Both complaints concern deletion requests that the consumers allege were submitted in October 2024 and not honored within the statutory timeframe. The response deadline is March 18, 2025 (30 business days from receipt). The deletion-request-delay issue identified in the Thornbury Risk Advisors LLP audit --- which documented an average processing time of 68 calendar days, with 22% of requests exceeding the statutory timeline even when accounting for the single permissible 45-day extension --- is directly relevant to the substance of this inquiry.

131	**[4. Regulatory Updates and Advisory Opinions]{.underline}**
132	
133	**4.1 Updated CPPA Regulations (Finalized March 29, 2024; Effective July 1, 2024)**
134	
135	The CPPA finalized its updated package of regulations on March 29, 2024, following an extensive public comment period and multiple rounds of revision. The updated regulations took effect on July 1, 2024, and now constitute the binding regulatory framework governing CPRA compliance. The key provisions of the updated regulations relevant to CHG\'s operations are summarized below.
136	
137	**Opt-out preference signals (§ 7025).** The updated regulations clarified that businesses must treat opt-out preference signals, including Global Privacy Control, as valid requests to opt out of the sale and sharing of personal information. Businesses may not require additional verification from consumers who send a GPC signal. Upon detecting the signal, the business must process it and cease sale and sharing for that consumer without requiring any further action on the consumer\'s part. The regulations also specify that a business must apply the opt-out preference to all personal information collected during the browsing session and any subsequent sessions associated with the same browser or device, unless and until the consumer affirmatively opts back in.
138	
139	**Dark patterns (§ 7004).** The regulations codified the definition of dark patterns and provided detailed examples of prohibited interface designs. Specifically, the regulations enumerate asymmetric choice architecture in consent flows as a paradigmatic dark pattern and provide illustrative examples that closely track the consent banner designs targeted in the CPPA\'s November 2024 enforcement sweep.
140	
141	**Service provider and contractor obligations (§§ 7050--7053).** The updated regulations strengthened requirements for written agreements between businesses and their service providers and contractors. Mandatory provisions now include certifications that the service provider or contractor understands and will comply with CPRA restrictions on data use, that it will not sell or share the personal information received, and that it will cooperate with the business in responding to consumer rights requests, including deletion, access, and correction requests. The regulations specify that businesses must flow down consumer request obligations to service providers and contractors through contractual provisions and must be able to demonstrate compliance with these requirements upon request by the CPPA.
142	
143	**Consumer request processing timelines.** The regulations reiterated the 45-calendar-day response deadline for consumer rights requests, with a single permissible 45-calendar-day extension available only when \"reasonably necessary\" and accompanied by written notice to the consumer within the initial 45-day period explaining the reason for the delay. The maximum total processing time is 90 calendar days from receipt of the request.
144	
145	**Sensitive personal information (SPI) disclosures.** The regulations reinforced that businesses collecting and processing sensitive personal information must provide a clear and conspicuous \"Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information\" link on their website and must disclose the categories of SPI collected and the purposes for which it is used in their privacy policy.
146	
147	**CHG relevance.** These regulations create binding compliance obligations that supersede any ambiguity that may have existed under the original CCPA framework. The GPC signal requirements are now unambiguous. The dark-patterns definition is now codified. The service provider and contractor agreement requirements are strengthened and clarified, rendering CHG\'s nine outdated DPAs --- which reference the pre-CPRA CCPA framework and therefore do not contain the mandated certifications --- demonstrably noncompliant. Businesses that updated their practices only to CCPA standards (pre-CPRA amendment) are now clearly noncompliant with the current regulatory framework.
148	
149	**4.2 Advisory Opinion on \"Sharing\" for Cross-Context Behavioral Advertising (October 15, 2024)**
150	
151	On October 15, 2024, the CPPA issued a formal advisory opinion addressing the scope of \"sharing\" under California Civil Code § 1798.140(ah). The advisory opinion was prompted by a pattern of inquiries from businesses and industry groups seeking clarification on whether certain data-transfer arrangements constituted \"sharing\" under CPRA.
152	
153	**Definition of \"sharing.\"** Under CPRA, \"sharing\" is defined as \"sharing, renting, releasing, disclosing, disseminating, making available, transferring, or otherwise communicating orally, in writing, or by electronic or other means, a consumer\'s personal information by the business to a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising, whether or not for monetary or other valuable consideration\" (Civil Code § 1798.140(ah)). The definition is notable for its breadth and for the fact that it applies regardless of whether the business receives any form of compensation in return.
154	
155	**Key clarification.** The CPPA explicitly stated in the advisory opinion that a business\'s act of making personal information available to a third party for purposes of cross-context behavioral advertising constitutes \"sharing\" under the statute, regardless of whether the business receives monetary compensation in return. The advisory opinion addressed a common misperception among businesses that \"sharing\" requires a direct exchange of consideration. The CPPA clarified that the exchange of monetary or other valuable consideration is the hallmark of a \"sale\" under § 1798.140(ad), not \"sharing.\" Sharing is defined by the purpose of the data transfer --- specifically, whether the data is provided for cross-context behavioral advertising --- not by whether compensation changes hands.
156	
157	**Cross-context behavioral advertising defined.** The advisory opinion reiterated the statutory definition: cross-context behavioral advertising means the targeting of advertising to a consumer based on personal information obtained from the consumer\'s activity across businesses, distinctly-branded websites, applications, or services, other than the business with which the consumer intentionally interacts (Civil Code § 1798.140(k)).
158	
159	**Practical implications.** The advisory opinion stated that businesses providing personal information to advertising networks, audience platforms, or data analytics firms for purposes of building audience segments, lookalike models, or targeted advertising campaigns are engaged in \"sharing\" even if: (a) the business characterizes the arrangement as a \"service provider\" relationship; (b) the business does not receive direct monetary compensation; or (c) the business frames the data transfer as necessary for the business\'s own marketing purposes. The CPPA noted that the characterization of the contractual relationship is not dispositive; rather, the controlling factor is the use to which the data is put by the receiving party. If the receiving party uses the data for cross-context behavioral advertising, the transfer constitutes sharing under the statute.
160	
161	**Obligations triggered by \"sharing.\"** When a business engages in \"sharing\" as defined by the statute, it must:
162	
163	> \(i\) provide consumers with the right to opt out of sharing, via either a standalone \"Do Not Share My Personal Information\" link or a combined \"Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information\" link on its homepage and in its privacy policy;
164	>
165	> \(ii\) disclose the sharing in its privacy policy, including the categories of personal information shared and the categories of third parties with whom it is shared;
166	>
167	> \(iii\) honor opt-out preference signals, including GPC, as valid opt-out-of-sharing requests; and
168	>
169	> \(iv\) ensure that any third-party recipient of shared data is contractually bound to use the data only for the disclosed business purposes and not for any other commercial purpose.
170	
171	**CHG relevance.** This advisory opinion has direct implications for CHG\'s data-sharing arrangements with AdVantage Digital Networks (\"ADN\") and Prism Audience Solutions (\"Prism\"). CHG provides loyalty program data --- including name, email address, phone number, physical address, purchase history, and browsing behavior --- from the approximately 412,000 enrolled California Cascadia Rewards members to ADN and Prism for purposes of targeted advertising campaigns and audience lookalike modeling. CHG receives \$1.4 million annually from ADN and \$860,000 annually from Prism (a combined total of \$2.26 million per year) in exchange for this data access. Under the framework established by this advisory opinion, CHG\'s data-transfer arrangements with ADN and Prism constitute both \"sale\" (due to the monetary consideration exchanged, under § 1798.140(ad)) and \"sharing\" (due to the cross-context behavioral advertising purpose, under § 1798.140(ah)). CHG is therefore subject to both sets of statutory obligations, including the provision of opt-out rights, privacy policy disclosures, and the honoring of GPC signals as valid opt-out-of-sharing requests.
172	
173	**4.3 Other Notable CPPA Guidance and Statements (2023--2025)**
174	
175	The following is a brief compilation of additional CPPA public statements, FAQ updates, and informal guidance documents issued between 2023 and 2025 that are relevant to CHG\'s compliance posture.
176	
177	**Consumer request processing guidance (2023).** The CPPA published FAQs clarifying that the 45-calendar-day clock for responding to consumer rights requests begins when the request is received by the business, regardless of the method of submission (whether via online portal, phone, email, in-person, or any other channel). Businesses cannot restart the clock by subsequently requesting identity verification. The clock begins on the date of receipt of the initial request; time spent verifying the consumer\'s identity runs concurrently with the response period.
178	
179	**Sensitive personal information guidance (2024).** The CPPA provided clarification that \"precise geolocation\" --- defined as any data derived from a device that is used or intended to be used to locate a consumer within a geographic area equal to or less than the area of a circle with a radius of 1,750 feet (approximately one-third of a mile) --- is classified as sensitive personal information (\"SPI\") under Civil Code § 1798.140(ae). Businesses that collect precise geolocation data must provide consumers with the right to limit the use and disclosure of their SPI under Civil Code § 1798.121 and must display a clear and conspicuous \"Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information\" link on their website and mobile application.
180	
181	**Service provider vs. third party distinction (2024).** The CPPA clarified in published guidance that a vendor receiving personal information from a business is classified as a \"service provider\" or \"contractor\" only if there is a qualifying written agreement in place that meets the requirements of Civil Code § 1798.140(ag) (for service providers) or § 1798.140(j) (for contractors). The agreement must contain the specific provisions and certifications mandated by the statute and the updated regulations. Without such a qualifying agreement, the recipient is classified as a \"third party,\" and the transfer of personal information to that recipient may constitute a \"sale\" or \"sharing\" under the statute, triggering opt-out rights, disclosure obligations, and other requirements.
182	
183	**Employee data (2023).** The CPPA confirmed in a public statement that the employee and HR data exemption under the original CCPA (former Civil Code § 1798.145(m)(1)) expired on January 1, 2023. Personal information collected in the employment context, including data from job applicants, current employees, and former employees, is now fully subject to CPRA rights and obligations, including the rights of access, deletion, correction, and opt-out.
184	
185	**CHG relevance.** Each of these guidance items has relevance to specific CHG compliance areas. The precise geolocation SPI guidance is relevant to CHG\'s sharing of mobile app geolocation data with Locale Metrics Inc. The service provider versus third-party distinction guidance is directly relevant to the nine outdated vendor DPAs: without CPRA-compliant agreements in place, CHG\'s vendors under those outdated agreements may be reclassified as \"third parties,\" converting routine data transfers into unlawful \"sales\" or \"sharing\" and triggering obligations that CHG is not currently meeting. The employee data confirmation is relevant to CHG\'s approximately 380 California-based employees whose personal information is now subject to the full suite of CPRA requirements.

216	
217	The CPPA listed dark patterns in consent flows as its fourth 2025 enforcement priority, building on the November 2024 enforcement sweep described in Section 3.3 above. The CPPA stated that it intends to expand its focus beyond cookie consent banners to include all privacy-related choice interfaces, encompassing opt-out mechanisms, privacy preference centers, account deletion flows, and data access request portals.

219	The CPPA specifically identified the following practices as continued enforcement targets for 2025:
220	
221	> • **Asymmetric choice architecture:** Interfaces where the privacy-invasive option (e.g., \"Accept All\") is visually dominant while the privacy-protective option (e.g., \"Reject All\" or \"Manage Preferences\") is visually minimized.
222	>
223	> • **Absence of a \"Reject All\" option:** Interfaces that offer an \"Accept All\" option but do not provide an equally prominent and easily accessible \"Reject All\" option.

227	> • **Confirmshaming:** The use of language designed to guilt, embarrass, or emotionally manipulate consumers into maintaining data collection settings (e.g., \"No thanks, I don\'t care about saving money\").

257	**5.7 Priority 6: Right-to-Delete Compliance Timelines**
258	
259	The CPPA identified right-to-delete compliance timelines as its sixth 2025 enforcement priority. 260	
261	The statutory framework requires businesses to respond to verified deletion requests within 45 calendar days of receipt. A single 45-calendar-day extension is permitted if \"reasonably necessary,\" but the business must notify the consumer in writing within the initial 45-day period, providing the reason for the delay and the expected completion date. 269	**[6. Enforcement Trends and Analytical Observations]{.underline}**
270	
271	**6.1 Pattern: Sweep-Based Enforcement Model**
272	
273	The CPPA has adopted a sweep-based enforcement model, targeting specific compliance areas across multiple companies simultaneously rather than pursuing individual, one-off enforcement cases. This approach serves several strategic purposes: it maximizes the deterrent effect of enforcement activity, establishes consistent enforcement standards across an industry or compliance area, and generates public attention that motivates broader industry compliance beyond the specific companies targeted. For CHG, the implication is that even if the company is not currently the subject of a specific sweep investigation, its practices may be identified through automated testing tools, consumer complaints, industry-wide reviews, or referrals from other enforcement actions.
274	
275	**6.2 Pattern: Escalating Penalties**
276	
277	The trajectory of CPPA enforcement suggests a clear trend of escalating penalties. The first enforcement sweep (August 2024, GPC signals) resulted in \$1.85 million in combined fines across three companies, with individual settlements ranging from \$250,000 to \$950,000. The CPPA has signaled repeatedly that future enforcement actions may calculate fines on a per-violation (per-consumer) basis rather than the negotiated per-business basis used in the initial settlements.
278	
279	The statutory maximum of \$2,500 per violation (\$7,500 per intentional violation) creates enormous theoretical exposure for businesses with large California consumer bases. Applied to CHG\'s approximately 1.62 million annual California consumers, even a narrow subset of violations could produce exposure in the tens of millions of dollars. By way of illustration, if the CPPA were to calculate GPC-related fines on a per-consumer basis for just the 195,000 California mobile app users, the theoretical maximum exposure at \$2,500 per violation would be \$487.5 million. While negotiated settlements typically reflect a substantial discount from statutory maximums, the magnitude of theoretical exposure underscores the importance of early, voluntary remediation and good-faith cooperation with the CPPA as the most effective strategy for mitigating penalty risk.
280	
281	**6.3 Pattern: Multi-Issue Investigations**
282	
283	The CPPA\'s Inquiry Letter process typically begins with a narrow scope tied to specific consumer complaints, but investigations frequently expand when the agency\'s review of the business\'s response reveals broader compliance issues. The document requests in a standard Inquiry Letter --- including requests for written policies and procedures, vendor lists, and evidence of downstream deletion --- are designed to provide the CPPA with a window into the business\'s overall compliance posture, not merely the specific complaints at issue.
284	
285	In CHG\'s case, the Inquiry Letter\'s request for written policies and procedures for handling deletion requests will likely expose the systemic 68-day average processing time and the 22% failure rate, issues that extend far beyond the two individual complaints. Similarly, the request for a vendor list and evidence of downstream deletion may surface the outdated DPA issue. CHG should anticipate that the Inquiry Letter response, if not carefully managed and strategically prepared, could trigger a broader investigation touching on multiple compliance areas, including GPC non-compliance, consent interface design, and data-sharing practices.

From : Maya Torsten <mtorsten@cascadiahomegoods.com>
To : Lars Engebretsen <lengebretsen@cascadiahomegoods.com>
Cc : Brian Hsu <bhsu@cascadiahomegoods.com>, Fiona Driscoll <fdriscoll@cascadiahomegoods.com>
Date : Sun, 09 Feb 2025 06:15:00 -0000
Subject : Re: CPPA Inquiry Letter — Need Alignment Before March 18 Deadline
Content-Type : text/plain; charset="utf-8"
Content-Transfer-Encoding : quoted-printable

---- text/plain None
Lars, Brian, Fiona —

Confirmed for tomorrow, Monday February 10 at 10 AM. Calendar invite is in your inboxes.

I've spent a good part of this weekend working through the issues raised in this thread, and I want to give you some preliminary answers so we can hit the ground running tomorrow.

**Outside Counsel / Privilege Strategy**

I agree with Lars — outside counsel should be engaged immediately, and budget should not be the gating factor here. I've already placed a call to Oakvale Hale LLP, specifically to their privacy and data security practice group. I'm expecting to hear back first thing Monday morning.

My strong recommendation is that the CPPA response be prepared under the supervision of outside counsel to preserve attorney-client privilege over our internal work product. This is especially important given the scope of what we've uncovered through the Thornbury audit. Critically, we need to be very deliberate about how we scope the response: we need to answer what the CPPA has asked — the two specific consumer complaints — without volunteering information about our broader compliance gaps. At the same time, we need to be truthful and avoid any misleading omissions. This is a fine line, and it's exactly why outside counsel should quarterback the response.

On the timing front — Lars, I hear you on not requesting an extension. I agree that would send the wrong signal. We'll hold the March 18 deadline.

I also want to flag that we should begin accelerating certain remediation steps now, independent of the response. If the CPPA follows up with additional questions or escalates to a formal investigation, being able to demonstrate that CHG identified these issues and began proactive remediation will significantly strengthen our position and could materially reduce any penalties. This is the "good faith" card, and we want to be able to play it.

**Data Sharing with ADN and Prism — Legal Analysis**

Responding to both Brian and Lars on this point. I've now reviewed the CPPA's October 15, 2024 advisory opinion in detail and cross-referenced it with our contractual arrangements. Here's my preliminary view:

Under the advisory opinion, CHG's data sharing with AdVantage Digital Networks and Prism Audience Solutions for targeted advertising and audience lookalike modeling almost certainly constitutes "sharing" as defined under Civil Code § 1798.140(ah). That provision covers making personal information available to a third party for cross-context behavioral advertising. This is true regardless of the fact that CHG also receives monetary compensation ($2.26M/year combined) — the "sharing" definition doesn't depend on whether money changes hands. The money actually makes it worse, not better, because it also likely qualifies as a "sale" under § 1798.140(ad).

The practical consequence: California consumers have the right to opt out of this sharing, and CHG is required to provide a "Do Not Share My Personal Information" link on its website (or a combined "Do Not Sell or Share" link). Currently, CHG has neither the link nor the opt-out mechanism. Brian — to answer your question directly — I don't think we're necessarily looking at an immediate shutdown of these partnerships, but we are looking at a scenario where we need to build an opt-out infrastructure, honor opt-out requests, and restructure how data flows to these partners. The revenue impact will depend on opt-out rates, which vary widely by industry, but we should model scenarios for Monday's discussion.

**Cascadia Rewards / Financial Incentive Exposure**

Lars, to your question about whether the loyalty program itself could become a regulatory target — yes, this is a real exposure.

Under CPRA's financial incentive provisions (Civil Code § 1798.125), when a business offers a loyalty program that collects personal information and derives economic benefit from that data — as CHG does through the ADN and Prism payments — the program may be treated as a "financial incentive." If so, CHG is required to post a "Notice of Financial Incentive" that explains the material terms of the incentive, the categories of personal information collected, and how the business has calculated the value of the consumer's data. CHG has no such notice. The Cascadia Rewards enrollment terms and our privacy policy are both silent on data monetization through advertising partnerships. Brian's instinct was right — our current terms don't mention anything about sharing data with advertising partners, and that's a problem.

I'd characterize this as a "sleeper issue." It hasn't appeared prominently in the CPPA's published enforcement priorities to date, but it could very easily be surfaced during an investigation into the data-sharing arrangements. Once the CPPA starts pulling on the ADN/Prism thread in the context of the two consumer complaints, the loyalty program's role as the data source is going to be immediately apparent. With 412,000 enrolled California members, the scale is significant.

**Briefing Memo**

The full briefing memo will cover all of the above in detail, including financial exposure calculations across each compliance gap, a prioritized remediation roadmap with costs and timelines, and a specific recommendation on the CPPA response strategy. I will have it ready for leadership by end of the week of February 10 — in time for Lars to prepare his board materials.

**For Tomorrow's Meeting**

Brian — please have the ADN and Prism data flow documentation ready. I need to understand exactly what data points are going to each partner, under what contractual terms, and what the consent/notice mechanism is at the point of collection.

Fiona — please bring the vendor DPA status tracker and the portal logs for the two consumers. The 72- and 74-day processing times plus the absence of extension notices are going to be central to our response, and I want to review the full documentation chain.

See everyone at 10 AM.

**Please treat this entire thread as privileged and confidential — attorney-client / work product. Do not forward outside the four of us.**

Best,

Maya Torsten
VP of Legal & Compliance / Privacy Officer
Cascadia Home Goods, Inc.
2250 NW Flanders Street, Suite 400
Portland, OR 97210
(503) 555-0149 | mtorsten@cascadiahomegoods.com

Both exceeded the 45-day statutory window, and — this is the part that concerns me most — neither consumer was sent a formal extension notice. Under CPRA, we would have needed to notify them within 45 days that we were invoking the extension, and we simply didn't. So we can't even argue we were operating within the extended 90-day window. We just blew the deadline.
>>

>>
>> Our customer data platform consolidates data from all touchpoints — e-commerce, in-store POS, mobile app, loyalty program, and 23 third-party vendor integrations. When a deletion request comes in, the current process requires manual identity verification, then deletion across the CDP, plus downstream deletion requests to every vendor and partner who received that consumer's data. With 34,000 California deletion requests per year flowing through this pipeline, the current process is strained well beyond capacity. The 68-day average processing time that Thornbury flagged isn't an anomaly — it's systemic. We don't have an automated orchestration layer for deletion workflows, and building one is a nontrivial engineering effort.
>>

Of our 23 vendor DPAs, 9 are from 2021 and do not include CPRA-compliant deletion-upon-request obligations. The contracts predate the CPRA regulations and were never updated. I'm not confident we have a contractual mechanism to compel deletion from all downstream recipients, which is what the CPPA is going to want to see.
>>
>> One more thing — while I was reviewing the audit findings to prep for this, I noticed the GPC signal issue and wanted to raise it since it's related to the broader remediation picture. Our current tag management system does not detect or act on Global Privacy Control signals from browsers. Implementing GPC recognition would require changes to the tag management configuration, the consent management platform, and the downstream data flows to ADN, Prism, and Locale Metrics Inc. I estimate this falls within the $185,000 platform remediation cost from the Thornbury estimate, but I want to be upfront: this could take 8–12 weeks to implement properly and test across all browser environments. We can't just flip a switch.
>>

I seem to recall the audit flagged something about geolocation and sensitive personal information. Maya, does this create any additional exposure we should be discussing?
>>
>> I'll have the full portal logs and data flow documentation for the two specific consumers ready by February 10. I'll also pull the vendor DPA status tracker — the spreadsheet my team maintains with contract dates, compliance status, and amendment history — for your review.

I've now had a chance to cross-reference the Inquiry Letter with the Thornbury Risk Advisors LLP privacy audit report completed January 15, 2025, and I want to flag that the situation is more complex than just two consumer complaints.
>>>>
>>>> **CPPA Inquiry Letter — Overview**
>>>>
>>>> The CPPA Enforcement Division sent the letter in response to two consumer complaints filed on December 10, 2024, and December 28, 2024. Both consumers allege that CHG failed to honor deletion requests they submitted via our online portal in October 2024.
>>>>

>>>>

>>>>

def bullet(text, level=0):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style="List Bullet" if level==0 else "List Bullet 2")
    runs(p, text); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(3); return p

def num(text):
    p = doc.add_paragraph(style="List Number"); runs(p, text); p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(3); return p

def table(headers, rows, widths=None, fs=9):
    t = doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(headers)); t.style = "Table Grid"; t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.CENTER
    for i,h in enumerate(headers):
        c = t.rows[0].cells[i]; c.text = ""; r = c.paragraphs[0].add_run(h); r.bold=True; r.font.size=Pt(fs); r.font.color.rgb=RGBColor(0xFF,0xFF,0xFF); shade(c,"1F3A5F")
    for row in rows:
        cells = t.add_row().cells
        for i,v in enumerate(row):
            cells[i].text = ""; p = cells[i].paragraphs[0]
            parts = str(v).split("**")
            for j,s in enumerate(parts):
                if s: rr = p.add_run(s); rr.bold = (j%2==1); rr.font.size = Pt(fs)
    if widths:
        for row in t.rows:
            for i,w in enumerate(widths): row.cells[i].width = Inches(w)
    doc.add_paragraph().paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
    return t

H1 = lambda t: doc.add_heading(t, level=1)
H2 = lambda t: doc.add_heading(t, level=2)

para("**The inquiry.** On February 3, 2025, the CPPA Enforcement Division (Deputy Director Rachel Mendoza-Park; assigned analyst Daniela Vargas, Senior Enforcement Analyst) issued an Inquiry Letter concerning two consumer complaints (filed December 10 and December 28, 2024) alleging that deletion requests submitted through our online portal in October 2024 were neither completed nor acknowledged, and that follow-up calls to our toll-free line (1-888-555-0147) were unproductive. # ---------- V ----------
H1("V. Issue-by-Issue Analysis and Required Actions")
H2("A. Deletion request processing (C-04) — active inquiry")
para("The 45-day clock runs from receipt regardless of channel; verification time runs concurrently and does not restart it; an extension requires written notice within the first 45 days stating the reason; and deletion must reach service providers and contractors, with notice to third parties to whom data was sold or shared (§ 1798.105(c)). The CPPA'"'"'s 2025 statement says it will examine completeness of deletion (including vendors), downstream notification, use of statutory exceptions, the adequacy of written procedures, and multi-step deletion flows that may themselves be dark patterns. Root causes: 2 FTEs for ~34,000 requests a year, manual compilation across the e-commerce platform, CDP, POS and loyalty database, no vendor-confirmation tracking, no workflow tooling, and a Q4 surge (October 2024 ≈ 4,200 requests — the month both complainants filed).")
bullet("Immediately: triage the open backlog; send compliant extension notices for every open request still inside day 45; complete all requests past day 90 first; brief the toll-free customer service team with a scripted status-response process.")
bullet("Within 2 weeks: add at least 2 FTEs (temporary or managed service) and adopt written deletion SOPs with day-30 and day-40 escalation and extension templates (dated as adopted — not back-dated).")
bullet("Within 6–8 weeks (Fiona to confirm): automated intake-to-completion workflow with vendor deletion instructions and confirmations logged per request.")
H2("B. Global Privacy Control (C-01)")
para("Section 7025 requires treating GPC as a valid opt-out of sale and sharing for that browser/device, without further consumer action, and applying it to later sessions. The CPPA says it can now detect non-compliance programmatically, so we should assume our site can be identified without a complaint. Fiona estimates **8–12 weeks** for full implementation across the tag manager (Silverdale), consent platform, and the ADN, Prism and Locale Metrics flows; Thornbury estimated 4–6 weeks. I recommend a two-step approach: an interim rule in the tag manager within 2–3 weeks that suppresses advertising/sharing tags (ADN, Prism, Canopy, Ashgrove, Oakmont, Harborview and similar) whenever Sec-GPC: 1 is present, followed by full CMP integration, server-side propagation to downstream partners, and app support.")
H2("C. Cookie consent dark patterns (C-02)")
para("Our banner has each feature the CPPA has called out: a dominant \"Accept All,\" no \"Reject All,\" a gray \"Manage Preferences\" link below the fold (60% of the mobile screen covered, link only reachable by scrolling), and non-essential categories pre-set to ON in the secondary panel. Consent obtained this way is not valid, which taints the cookie-based data flowing to advertising vendors. The fix is inexpensive and quick (2–3 weeks): symmetric Accept/Reject buttons, a visible Manage Preferences button, non-essential categories defaulted OFF, no obstructive overlay, mobile-visible choices. This should ship before the March 18 filing.")
H2("D. ADN / Prism data sharing and the Cascadia Rewards program")
para("Under the October 15, 2024 advisory opinion, making loyalty data available to ADN and Prism for audience lookalike modeling and cross-context behavioral advertising is \"sharing\" (§ 1798.140(ah)), and because CHG is paid it is also a \"sale\" (§ 1798.140(ad)). How the contract labels the counterparty (\"partner\") is not dispositive; our own tracker recommends classifying both as **third parties**. Consequences: a conspicuous \"Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information\" link (we have only a footer-only, pre-CPRA \"Do Not Sell\" link — M-11), GPC honored as an opt-out of both, privacy-policy disclosure of categories sold/shared and recipients, and third-party contract terms limiting use to specified purposes.")
para("**Brian'"'"'s consent question.** Enrollment in a points program does not supply consent or a defense: the terms never disclosed advertising data monetization, so there was no informed agreement; and consumers keep a statutory right to opt out of sale/sharing regardless of enrollment. Because the program collects personal information and CHG gets economic value from that data, Cascadia Rewards is likely a **financial incentive** under § 1798.125 requiring a Notice of Financial Incentive (material terms, categories of data, and a good-faith estimate of the value of the consumer'"'"'s data and how it was calculated — our tracker'"'"'s $5.49 per member per year is a starting point). There is none today. The data categories also need to be confirmed: Brian and the tracker list name, email, phone, mailing address, purchase history and browsing behavior (and loyalty tier for Prism); Thornbury lists fewer.")
para("**Recommended interim posture (Decision 4):** (i) confirm within one week that the ~3,500 sale opt-outs received in 2024 actually suppress ADN and Prism feeds, and suppress anyone with a pending or completed deletion request; (ii) deploy GPC suppression for these feeds; (iii) publish the updated notice, opt-out link and financial-incentive notice; (iv) execute CPRA third-party amendments (Prism auto-renewed January 9, 2025, so amendment must be negotiated mid-term; ADN renews June 14, 2025). If (i)–(iii) are not in place by **April 15, 2025**, pause the feeds until they are. Also confirm ADN and Prism are registered data brokers if the Delete Act applies to them.")
H2("E. Precise geolocation to Locale Metrics (sensitive personal information)")
para("Locale Metrics receives latitude/longitude accurate to about 50 feet (well inside the 1,750-foot SPI threshold), device IDs, visit timestamps and dwell time for ~195,000 California app users. The privacy policy and 2022-era app notice disclose none of this; there is no limit-SPI mechanism; and the 2021 DPA has no SPI terms or CPRA certifications. Without a qualifying contract, Locale Metrics is a third party, and because CHG supplies the data in exchange for analytics, the exchange risks being characterized as a sale for \"other valuable consideration.\" Actions: confirm whether Locale Metrics uses the data for any purpose of its own; execute a CPRA service-provider agreement limiting use to CHG'"'"'s foot-traffic reporting; add SPI disclosures and a \"Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information\" link (web and app) unless counsel concludes the use is limited to permitted purposes; and consider reducing precision or retention. Owner: Fiona with Legal; target April 15.")

# ---------- VI ----------
H1("VI. Recommended CPPA Inquiry Response Strategy")
H2("A. Recommendation")
para("**Respond fully, accurately and on time, under Oakvale Hale'"'"'s supervision, and pair the response with a credible description of remediation already under way on the deletion process.** I recommend against both an extension request (agreeing with Lars) and a narrowly lawyered response that withholds or shades responsive material. The letter'"'"'s requests (b)–(d) are designed to reveal how our program works; our policies, vendor list and lack of downstream deletion evidence will show the systemic issue whatever we say. Credibility at the inquiry stage is the most valuable mitigating factor we control, while evasiveness or later-discovered inaccuracy is an aggravating factor and could expose individuals and the company to far more serious consequences than the underlying violations.")
para("This refines my February 5 and 9 emails. It is legitimate to limit the response to what is asked and not to produce privileged material or volunteer unrelated findings (e.g., the GPC and banner findings). It is not acceptable to omit responsive documents, recast policies, or describe the two cases as isolated when our data show they are not, if the response would otherwise imply that. Counsel should make the final judgment on how much of the systemic deletion backlog to describe, but my recommendation is to acknowledge it at a general level together with the remediation plan, because request (b) will reveal it anyway.")

def runs(p, text):

H2("A. Deletion request processing (C-04) — active inquiry")
para("The 45-day clock runs from receipt regardless of channel; verification time runs concurrently and does not restart it; an extension requires written notice within the first 45 days stating the reason; and deletion must reach service providers and contractors, with notice to third parties to whom data was sold or shared (§ 1798.105(c)). The CPPA'"'"'s 2025 statement says it will examine completeness of deletion (including vendors), downstream notification, use of statutory exceptions, the adequacy of written procedures, and multi-step deletion flows that may themselves be dark patterns. Root causes: 2 FTEs for ~34,000 requests a year, manual compilation across the e-commerce platform, CDP, POS and loyalty database, no vendor-confirmation tracking, no workflow tooling, and a Q4 surge (October 2024 ≈ 4,200 requests — the month both complainants filed).")
bullet("Immediately: triage the open backlog; send compliant extension notices for every open request still inside day 45; complete all requests past day 90 first; brief the toll-free customer service team with a scripted status-response process.")
bullet("Within 2 weeks: add at least 2 FTEs (temporary or managed service) and adopt written deletion SOPs with day-30 and day-40 escalation and extension templates (dated as adopted — not back-dated).")
bullet("Within 6–8 weeks (Fiona to confirm): automated intake-to-completion workflow with vendor deletion instructions and confirmations logged per request.")
H2("B. Global Privacy Control (C-01)")
para("Section 7025 requires treating GPC as a valid opt-out of sale and sharing for that browser/device, without further consumer action, and applying it to later sessions. The CPPA says it can now detect non-compliance programmatically, so we should assume our site can be identified without a complaint. Fiona estimates **8–12 weeks** for full implementation across the tag manager (Silverdale), consent platform, and the ADN, Prism and Locale Metrics flows; Thornbury estimated 4–6 weeks. I recommend a two-step approach: an interim rule in the tag manager within 2–3 weeks that suppresses advertising/sharing tags (ADN, Prism, Canopy, Ashgrove, Oakmont, Harborview and similar) whenever Sec-GPC: 1 is present, followed by full CMP integration, server-side propagation to downstream partners, and app support.")
H2("C. Cookie consent dark patterns (C-02)")
para("Our banner has each feature the CPPA has called out: a dominant \"Accept All,\" no \"Reject All,\" a gray \"Manage Preferences\" link below the fold (60% of the mobile screen covered, link only reachable by scrolling), and non-essential categories pre-set to ON in the secondary panel. Consent obtained this way is not valid, which taints the cookie-based data flowing to advertising vendors. The fix is inexpensive and quick (2–3 weeks): symmetric Accept/Reject buttons, a visible Manage Preferences button, non-essential categories defaulted OFF, no obstructive overlay, mobile-visible choices. This should ship before the March 18 filing.")
H2("D. ADN / Prism data sharing and the Cascadia Rewards program")
para("Under the October 15, 2024 advisory opinion, making loyalty data available to ADN and Prism for audience lookalike modeling and cross-context behavioral advertising is \"sharing\" (§ 1798.140(ah)), and because CHG is paid it is also a \"sale\" (§ 1798.140(ad)). How the contract labels the counterparty (\"partner\") is not dispositive; our own tracker recommends classifying both as **third parties**. Consequences: a conspicuous \"Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information\" link (we have only a footer-only, pre-CPRA \"Do Not Sell\" link — M-11), GPC honored as an opt-out of both, privacy-policy disclosure of categories sold/shared and recipients, and third-party contract terms limiting use to specified purposes.")
para("**Brian'"'"'s consent question.** Enrollment in a points program does not supply consent or a defense: the terms never disclosed advertising data monetization, so there was no informed agreement; and consumers keep a statutory right to opt out of sale/sharing regardless of enrollment. Because the program collects personal information and CHG gets economic value from that data, Cascadia Rewards is likely a **financial incentive** under § 1798.125 requiring a Notice of Financial Incentive (material terms, categories of data, and a good-faith estimate of the value of the consumer'"'"'s data and how it was calculated — our tracker'"'"'s $5.49 per member per year is a starting point). There is none today. The data categories also need to be confirmed: Brian and the tracker list name, email, phone, mailing address, purchase history and browsing behavior (and loyalty tier for Prism); Thornbury lists fewer.")
para("**Recommended interim posture (Decision 4):** (i) confirm within one week that the ~3,500 sale opt-outs received in 2024 actually suppress ADN and Prism feeds, and suppress anyone with a pending or completed deletion request; (ii) deploy GPC suppression for these feeds; (iii) publish the updated notice, opt-out link and financial-incentive notice; (iv) execute CPRA third-party amendments (Prism auto-renewed January 9, 2025, so amendment must be negotiated mid-term; ADN renews June 14, 2025). If (i)–(iii) are not in place by **April 15, 2025**, pause the feeds until they are. Also confirm ADN and Prism are registered data brokers if the Delete Act applies to them.")
H2("E. Precise geolocation to Locale Metrics (sensitive personal information)")
para("Locale Metrics receives latitude/longitude accurate to about 50 feet (well inside the 1,750-foot SPI threshold), device IDs, visit timestamps and dwell time for ~195,000 California app users. The privacy policy and 2022-era app notice disclose none of this; there is no limit-SPI mechanism; and the 2021 DPA has no SPI terms or CPRA certifications. Without a qualifying contract, Locale Metrics is a third party, and because CHG supplies the data in exchange for analytics, the exchange risks being characterized as a sale for \"other valuable consideration.\" Actions: confirm whether Locale Metrics uses the data for any purpose of its own; execute a CPRA service-provider agreement limiting use to CHG'"'"'s foot-traffic reporting; add SPI disclosures and a \"Limit the Use of My Sensitive Personal Information\" link (web and app) unless counsel concludes the use is limited to permitted purposes; and consider reducing precision or retention. Owner: Fiona with Legal; target April 15.")

**PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL --- ATTORNEY-CLIENT COMMUNICATION / ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT**

Prepared at the direction of counsel in anticipation of a regulatory proceeding. Do not forward outside the addressees. Draft for review by Oakvale Hale LLP before any board circulation.

**EXECUTIVE BRIEFING MEMORANDUM**

  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  TO                                  Lars Engebretsen, Chief Executive Officer
  ----------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  CC                                  Brian Hsu, Chief Marketing Officer; Fiona Driscoll, Chief Technology Officer

  FROM                                Maya Torsten, VP of Legal & Compliance / Privacy Officer

  DATE                                February 14, 2025

  RE                                  CPRA compliance risks, financial exposure, and remediation priorities --- including response strategy for CPPA Inquiry Letter, Case No. CPPA-ENF-2025-01847 (response due March 18, 2025)
  -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# I. Bottom Line

CHG is exposed on **five of the CPPA\'s six announced 2025 enforcement priorities** at once (opt-out preference signals/GPC; dark patterns; service-provider/contractor agreements; right-to-delete timelines; and, through the privacy policy and loyalty program, the disclosure obligations that underpin all of them), and it has an **open CPPA inquiry** whose document requests will expose the deletion and vendor-contract problems regardless of how the response is framed. The two complaints are symptoms of a systemic deletion-processing failure that the Agency will see as soon as it reviews our policies and vendor list.

- **Most urgent (next 30 days):** (1) file a complete, accurate, on-time response to the Inquiry Letter (target submission **March 14**, four days before the March 18 deadline); (2) issue a document preservation notice today; (3) turn on GPC recognition and replace the cookie banner --- both are being detected by the CPPA with automated tools, are cheap to fix relative to exposure, and should be fixed before the Agency looks beyond the two complaints.

- **Realistic exposure** if the inquiry expands into a multi-issue investigation: on the order of **\$1.1 million to \$4.5 million** in negotiated penalties (counsel\'s planning estimate, Section IV), plus a multi-year compliance order. **Theoretical statutory maximums run into the tens or hundreds of millions** on any per-consumer theory and should be described to the board as leverage the Agency holds, not as a forecast.

- **Remediation cost:** Thornbury estimates **\$425,000**, which exceeds the current \$340,000 privacy allocation by \$85,000. That figure is understated (it omits the two additional request-processing hires, the loyalty-program financial-incentive notice, the HR data assessment, and a \$6,000 DPA cost variance; and the CTO\'s GPC timeline is twice Thornbury\'s). I recommend authorizing **up to \$600,000** for 2025 remediation, with a 15% contingency held centrally.

- **ADN/Prism partnerships (\$2.26 million/year):** no shutdown is legally required, but the arrangements are a **\"sale\" and \"sharing\"** that must be supported by opt-out rights, GPC, privacy-policy disclosure, a Notice of Financial Incentive for Cascadia Rewards, and third-party contracts. Assuming opt-out rates of 10--40%, the revenue impact is roughly **\$226,000--\$904,000/year** --- well below the realistic penalty range and far below Brian\'s \$3--4 million full-shutdown ROAS estimate.

- **Response strategy:** answer every request fully and truthfully, including ADN and Prism as **third-party** recipients (the letter expressly asks for third parties, not only service providers); produce the policies that actually existed (no back-dating); acknowledge the deletion-timeline failure for the two consumers and describe remediation already under way; do not produce the privileged Thornbury report or volunteer unrelated findings, but make no statement that is inaccurate or misleading by omission. Detail in Section VI.

- **Data integrity warning:** several figures in our internal materials conflict (vendor names, the 7,480 late-request figure, the GPC population, vendor cost totals). These must be reconciled before anything is sent to the CPPA or the board (Section VIII).

## Decisions requested from the CEO

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  **\#**            **Decision**                                                                                  **Recommendation**                                                                                                                     **Needed by**
  ----------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- -----------------
  1                 Approve supplemental privacy remediation budget                                               Authorize up to \$600,000 (vs. \$340,000 allocated); release first \$250,000 immediately                                               Feb 18

  2                 Confirm Oakvale Hale LLP engagement; route Thornbury follow-on work through counsel           Approve; counsel to quarterback CPPA response and privileged remediation work                                                          Feb 18

  3                 Approve immediate hire/contract of 2+ request-processing FTEs (or a managed-service vendor)   Approve; temporary staff within 2 weeks                                                                                                Feb 21

  4                 Interim posture on ADN/Prism data feeds                                                       Continue only with interim controls (Section V.D); pause feeds if controls are not live by April 15                                    Feb 21

  5                 Board briefing (last week of February)                                                        Present this memo\'s summary, the realistic exposure range, and the remediation plan; schedule a follow-up after the March 18 filing   Feb 24
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# II. Background and Key Dates

**The inquiry.** On February 3, 2025, the CPPA Enforcement Division (Deputy Director Rachel Mendoza-Park; assigned analyst Daniela Vargas, Senior Enforcement Analyst) issued an Inquiry Letter concerning two consumer complaints (filed December 10 and December 28, 2024) alleging that deletion requests submitted through our online portal in October 2024 were neither completed nor acknowledged, and that follow-up calls to our toll-free line (1-888-555-0147) were unproductive. The letter cites the 45-day response period and single 45-day extension under Civil Code § 1798.130(a)(2), copies the Attorney General\'s Privacy Enforcement Section, and warns that an untimely or incomplete response may result in a formal investigation under § 1798.199.45 and fines of up to \$2,500 per violation or \$7,500 per intentional violation. It is not a finding of violation, and the Agency states that cooperation will be considered.

**What our own records show.** Fiona\'s review of the portal logs confirms that both requests were acknowledged 8 business days after submission (within the 10-business-day confirmation requirement), but deletion took **72 and 74 calendar days**, and **neither consumer received an extension notice**. Both requests were therefore late under § 1798.130(a)(2); we cannot rely on the 90-day extended window. Separately, Thornbury\'s January 15, 2025 audit found 17 issues (5 Critical, 12 Moderate) and a 68-day average deletion processing time.
